A.summary: A policy class (workspace.py) over a module of free functions (fsops.py) that walk each path one component at a time from a freshly opened root fd with O_NOFOLLOW and write by exclusive temp + os.replace. Read protection keeps both normalised names and (dev, ino) identities, plus a blanket refusal of hard-linked targets; there is no Location value or held root handle.

A.best_thing: Two layers: fsops knows only descriptors and links, and Workspace knows only policy, so every OS call goes through one module (impl-A/jailfs/fsops.py:1-15).
A.worst_thing: save() is one long method with its locator inlined, so remove() and any later write operation must copy it (impl-A/jailfs/workspace.py:275-292).

B.summary: A RootHandle class (handle.py) holds one directory fd per root and reports path problems as code-free Problem kinds. Workspace (workspace.py) turns those into refusals and holds _Root/_Location values, identity opened/written sets and a stack of per-batch saved-name sets; a mutation script proves each hole test.

A mutation script proves 14 hole tests, and a threaded test checks atomicity.

Agent absolute paths go through realpath, and roots are neither held open nor checked for overlap.

root held as an open fd object (RootHandle/Root)
identity opened set with a written exemption taken after the rename
given/real root spellings matched lexically; agent path never resolved
save order: link/shape, then duplicate, then shadow, then opened
mutation script proving each hole test

generativity.notes: All five converge on the core (fd walk, O_NOFOLLOW, exclusive temp + rename, a load that is a read). B, C and D share the chapter's full participant set, including the written exemption and the same check order, and differ in packaging: B has a code-free Problem layer, C has a separate lexical paths module and CLI-worded fixes, D is one file with numbered checks. A reaches similar safety without a Location or a held handle and adds name-based protection and a hard-link refusal. E departs where the chapter's notes are subtle (never resolve the agent's path, disjoint roots, identity) and spends its structure on a second backend. None of the five puts reads into the batch, so the next change reshapes batch state everywhere.

worse_is_better: D reaches B's and C's safety and proof with no separate handle module, no Root/RootHandle double wrapper and no Location in the public API. Its only extras are a few unused helpers (Root.label, describe). B and C carry a handle layer that the task's size does not need. A is smaller still and nearly as safe, but it reopens the root by path and has no proof tests. E carries the most extra machinery (a second backend, as_dict, backend_name, Windows drive letters), and none of it is needed: the task targets a stdlib with dir_fd, and the extra code coexists with the two real holes. The identity opened set is mostly redundant once links are refused and writes are rename-only, because a hard link's other name keeps its old content. A normalised-name set (A's _read_paths) gives the same guarantee, provided the agent's path is never resolved.
chapter_lessons: Say 'resolve root spellings once at start-up; never resolve the agent's path' as a rule, not only implicitly. E realpaths agent paths (impl-E/jailfs/workspace.py:233) and writes through an in-root link. Note 7 ('make a symlinked read root resolve to its target') reads as an invitation to do so. B, C and D each needed a dedicated mutation to guard against it.

Name disjoint roots as a start-up check. Four implementations invented it independently (impl-A/jailfs/workspace.py:121, impl-B/jailfs/workspace.py:147, impl-C/jailfs/workspace.py:109, impl-D/jailfs/workspace.py:229). The one that did not (E) lets a save overwrite a read root nested in the writable root.

Say what file identity buys once writes are rename-only and links are refused. Rename never writes through a hard link, so the opened-set-by-identity mostly repeats a name check. A refuses all hard links anyway (impl-A/jailfs/workspace.py:334), and E falls back to names. The chapter's 'unless the session wrote that file itself' exemption was copied by B, C and D and contradicts the task's 'would replace a file this session read'; A and E took the task's version. One rule should be chosen.

Make 'the run' a participant holding both saves and reads. The chapter scopes the opened set to the session and duplicates to one call. Every implementation models batch() as a bare set of saved names, so the next change (E_IN_USE for a file read in the same batch) reshapes batch state in all five.

State the root handle's lifetime: hold it open from start-up. A and E reopen the root by path on every call (impl-A/jailfs/fsops.py:124, impl-E/jailfs/fsio.py:175). A follows a root swapped for a link; E has to re-check it.

Phrase the strict-flags force in terms of configuration, not CLI flags. C copied '--read DIR' into the fixes of a Python constructor (impl-C/jailfs/workspace.py:67). D over-applied strictness to reads='dir' (impl-D/jailfs/workspace.py:186).

Repeat the 'no root-relative operations: isolate at process level, not with string checks' rule where implementers will see it. E built a weaker lstat backend anyway (impl-E/jailfs/fsio.py:361-515), which doubles every change.
